title: Fix the last commit
brief:
Welcome to Act 4: rewriting. Everything so far treated history as permanent. It is not: it is just expensive to change once shared. Until it is shared, it is yours.

You just committed `app.txt` as "add app v1", but you forgot `config.txt` and the message should say so. A second commit would tell the story of your mistake; nobody needs that story.

Create `config.txt` in the editor (content `debug = false`), stage it, then redo the last commit in place: `git commit --amend -m "add app v1 with config"`. Watch the graph: the old commit does not vanish, it fades. Amend replaces; nothing moves.
hints: Create config.txt with the editor's new-file button, stage it, then amend.
git add config.txt, then git commit --amend -m "add app v1 with config".
Amend builds a NEW commit with the old commit's parent and swaps the branch to it. The ghost on the graph is the original.
solution: git commit --amend -m "add app v1 with config"
